title: Short Stuff: Flower Power
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the origins and evolution of "flower power." Its roots trace to 1965 Berkeley free-speech protests, where Allen Ginsberg advised students to counter authority with silly, visual spectacle such as flowers, toy soldiers and candy, rather than follow the rules of confrontation. The idea moved to anti-Vietnam War protests, culminating in the 1967 march on the Pentagon, where Bernie Boston of the Washington Star photographed George Harris placing a daisy in the barrel of a National Guard/Reserve troop's M14 rifle. In 1967 San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury scene, flower power shifted from political protest toward fashion, music and countercultural lifestyle, and was commercialized. Hippies held a mock funeral for the hippie in October 1967 and burned the Psychedelic Shop sign. Scott McKenzie's hit "San Francisco" helped spread the image to mainstream America. The episode closes with a credit to Kristen Conger, who originally wrote the piece for HowStuffWorks.

segments.title: Opening and two flower power movements
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic and distinguish a 1967-68 political protest flower power from a later, more fashion and music oriented one centered in San Francisco.

segments.title: Ginsberg's advice to Berkeley protesters
segments.summary: In 1965 Allen Ginsberg, a Beat-turned-hippie figure, advised Berkeley students protesting campus speech limits. He wrote an essay on spectacle as communication, urging them to answer war-style intimidation with silliness and visual spectacle such as flowers, toy soldiers and candy, anticipating counter-protest from the Hells Angels.

segments.title: Pentagon march and the daisy photo
segments.summary: The idea carried into anti-Vietnam War protest. At the 1967 Pentagon march, Bernie Boston of the Washington Star photographed 18-year-old George Harris placing a daisy in the barrel of an M14 held by one of roughly 2,500 Reserve troops, creating an iconic image.

segments.title: From protest to San Francisco fashion trend
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck describe how flower power shifted from political protest to a cultural and fashion movement in San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury, with a focus on peace, love and clothing. Josh says the movement was co-opted and commercialized, and that the trend reached mainstream fashion.

segments.title: Psychedelic Shop and the hippie funeral
segments.summary: The Psychedelic Shop in Haight-Ashbury sold education on psychedelics before LSD was criminalized in California. Anti-commercialization hippies held a mock funeral for the hippie in October 1967, and burned the shop's sign. Josh also mentions a link to the Biosphere episode.

segments.title: Scott McKenzie's song and mainstream spread
segments.summary: Chuck notes Scott McKenzie's 1967 hit San Francisco, which the hosts say helped spread flower power to mainstream America, though the hosts do not say how the song contributed to the image beyond that.

segments.title: Reflections on the photo and credit to Kristen Conger
segments.summary: The hosts reflect on the courage of the daisy photo's subject and credit Kristen Conger, former colleague and host of Unladylike, who originally wrote the piece for HowStuffWorks.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Standard closing credits: Stuff You Should Know is an iHeartRadio production, with a pointer to the iHeartRadio app and podcast platforms.
